title.en: A Tale About Two Girls: Eagle and Whale Husbands

region.en: Coast and bird cliff, Greenland-Labrador copies
region.zh: 海岸與鳥崖（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; constructed from two manuscripts (Labrador and Greenland, before 1828), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Playing with eagle-bones and whale-bones, two girls boast — 'I will have an eagle for my husband' and 'I will have a whale for mine' — and are instantly taken, one to a cliff top, one to the sealed bottom of the sea. The eagle's bride knots a sinew string down to sea level and is rescued by a passing kayaker, the eagle shot when tricked into spreading his wings; the whale's bride, kept picking whale-lice and roped to a stone, is fetched by brothers who built a gull-beating umiak, throwing jackets into the pursuer's jaws until the shore is reached and the whale turns to a piece of whalebone.
summary.zh: 兩個小女孩在灘上玩鷹骨與鯨骨，各自誇口：『我要嫁鷹』『我要嫁鯨』——話音未落，一個被鷹掠上崖頂，一個被鯨拖入封閉的海底。鷹妻編鳥筋繩垂至海面，由過路皮艇客救出；鷹受騙展翅而被射殺。鯨妻被繩繫石上、日日揀鯨蝨；其兄以快過海鷗的大舟來救，她解繩繫石而逃，將外衣內衣逐一擲入鯨口拖延，抵岸之際鯨化為一片鯨骨。

sensitivity.note: Animal-husband type; variant of the same tale as Rasmussen's 'The Eagle and the Whale' (cross-ref inuit-eagle-and-whale) and Rink tale 12.

passages.text: Two little girls were playing with small bones on the beach, the one with eagle-bones, the other with whale-bones. Suddenly an eagle came soaring above them, and one of the girls said, 'I will have an eagle for my husband'; the other replied, 'Thou mayst rejoice that thou hast already got a husband; I will have a whale for mine.' Instantly a whale was seen to spout out at sea. The eagle took one girl up and flew away with her, and the whale took the other down to the bottom of the sea, having first made her eyes and ears impenetrable so that the water could not enter. The eagle carried his bride to the top of a steep cliff and brought her different sorts of little birds for food; but she gathered all the sinews of the birds' wings, knotted them together to make a string, and one day, when the eagle was away, found that it reached down to the level of the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another day she saw a kayaker rowing along the shore and called out to him to send a boat to rescue her; soon afterwards the boat appeared, and she went sliding down by her string of sinews and got back to her parents. The eagle, missing his mate, soared above the houses beating his wings, and one of the inhabitants cried out to him, 'If thou wantest to show thou hast been married into our family, spread out thy wings' — and when the eagle did so they shot him through the body. The other girl, secured to the bottom of the sea by a rope, had nothing to do but sit picking the lice from off the whale's body. Her two brothers set about building a boat of immense swiftness to deliver their sister; when finished, it could not match a bird in speed and was broken to pieces, another begun — that one matched a flying bird but was discarded, and a third outdid even the gull.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They started from home to fetch back their sister. Becoming aware of their approach, she loosened the cord that held her, twisted it round the stone, and left with the boat. When the whale on his return drew the cord and discovered she was gone, he hurried after her; coming quite close to the boat, she threw her outer jacket into the water. Having snapped at it he let it go and pursued again; quite close up with them, she flung her inner jacket, which again detained the whale — but he reached them a third time. Then she threw her long jacket, and before he could overtake them they had landed; when the whale reached the shore he was transformed into a piece of whalebone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Brothers Visit Their Cannibal Sister

region.en: South Greenland (winter station beyond the high mountains)
region.zh: 南格陵蘭（高山以南的越冬地）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; very popular in Greenland, literal translation from a single South Greenland manuscript, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Told late that they have a sister beyond the southern mountains — white-haired on one side and living among cannibals — two brothers travel by night to her house of three windows. A tub of berries mixed with blubber holds a shrunk human hand clutching the berries; she has turned cannibal because, she says, 'this nasty fellow has made me one.' The brother-in-law warns of sledge-lashings cut by his children, gives the shout that turns the settlement out black with people, then kills the lone pursuing sledge-driver and returns home freighted with human limbs — while the brothers escape and never see their sister again.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟成人後才得知：高山以南有位單側白髮的姐姐，嫁入食人族。他們趁夜抵達其三窗之屋；漿果拌脂油的大木桶底，竟見一隻枯縮斷腕抓握著莓果——姐姐承認自己已食人：『是這可憎的傢伙把我變成這樣。』姐夫早命孩子割斷鄰人雪橇繩索，送客出門一聲大喊，全村黑壓壓湧出——雪橇盡數散架，唯獨一輛追來，被他殺死車主、滿載人肢而歸。兄弟們逃出生天，從此再未見過姐姐。

sensitivity.note: Rink translated a single South Greenland manuscript nearly literally. Cannibalism recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A man had three children, the eldest a daughter, who married a man from a far-away place in the south while her brothers were still little; in their boyhood they did not know they had a sister, their father purposely never mentioning it, and even grown and catching seals they had never heard of her until one day the mother said, 'I think ye don't even know that ye have got a sister!' Asked where she lived, she answered: 'Look there; do you see the high mountains yonder to the south of us? Beyond these is the winter station of your sister, whose hair, strange to say, is quite white on one side. However, ye must not think of going there, for the people she is living among are all cannibals.' The eldest brother gave up the idea; the younger longed as much as ever, and despite the parents' warning — if ye reach the country in the day-time, wait the fall of night and go near only when they are all asleep, lest ye be murdered — the brothers set out, and the parents gave them up for lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Reaching the high mountains in the south they examined the land below for houses — 'When people are found to be living at the foot of the mountains, the ravens will be sure to be soaring in the air above' — until above a craggy hill a great number of ravens were flying. They secured their sledges and waited the fall of night; quite dark, they drew near many houses, the first with three windows, mounted the roof cautiously, and looked down the vent-hole: a nasty-looking man sat in front of the lamp beside his wife, who seemed to be picking lice off him and appeared quite white on one side of her head. 'Were we not told that our sister was to be white-haired on one side of her head? Do come and see!' The younger bade him spit down through the hole before the lamp; the moment he did, the woman pushed the man: 'Somebody must have come from afar to see us; do make haste and get up!' He rose, took his bow ready bent, and went outside — to be accosted before he had set eyes on them: 'We have come here to visit our sister, and have been told that she is quite white on one side of her head.' Whispering 'Your sister is within; please go in,' he at once played the part of a brother-in-law and ordered a meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The guests understood the only housemates of their sister were her children, the boot-drying beams hung with boots and skin-stockings of all sizes. A large tub of berries mingled with blubber was set before them, and the brothers, almost beginning to feel at ease, caught sight in the bottom of the tub of a human hand cut off at the wrist, clutching the berries, very much shrunk. 'We don't eat such food as this' — but she only drew the tub closer and began to eat along with the children; taking hold of the hand and biting the thumb, the children all cried, 'Mother, do let us have some too!' The eldest brother went close beside her: 'Hast thou also turned cannibal?' — and giving her husband a pull, she answered, 'This nasty fellow has made me one.' The brother-in-law ordered something separate cooked on the lamp, cautioning them not to let it burn too high lest the neighbours detect and make a row about it, and told how, when their people caught a whale last winter, a man happened to have a fall and was cut up with it. Before the meal he whispered to his children, 'Go out and cut asunder all the lashings of our neighbours' sledges, but beware of making a noise' — all done, though one was forgotten.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The host said that as soon as they finished he would accompany them a little way off, and that when they had left the mainland he would give a shout: 'Ye'll just see what will happen.' Seeing them off in their sledges, he cried out aloud as they turned onto the ice, 'The visitors are setting off — the visitors are going to leave!' — and when the brothers looked around, the place was black with people crowding the doorways and windows, some having just caught hold of their clothes, others quite naked, hastening off to their sledges; but when they were about to start, the sledges all broke down. The travellers took fright and urged on their dogs; one sledge, however, was following and apparently gaining, and the brother-in-law, hastening to pursue it, killed the driver besides a number of the other people, and afterwards filled his sledge with human limbs — thus freighted returning to his house. The brothers reached home late at night and reported how their sister had turned a cannibal and how they had barely escaped death through the aid of their brother-in-law; but they never saw their sister again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.

title.en: Kunuk the Orphan Boy: Brothers, Giants, and the Great Plain
title.zh: 孤兒庫努克：兄弟、巨人與大平原

region.en: Fiord entrance and southern giant-land (legendary migration route)
region.zh: 峽灣口與南方巨人之地（傳說遷徙路線）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; constructed from three copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two obliging orphan boys see an armed host advancing in the water-drawing moonlight, hide their little sister in wood-chips, and climb the rafters — seven raiders slaughter the household and spear the hidden girl. Carrying her corpse until they bury it in a cave, they train into stone-throwing, bear-crushing champions, marry the daughters of a wronged old man, harden their bodies against the chief's walrus-skin whip, kill him with his own trick, free the village — 'In future ye shall have no masters' — then sail south to destroy the giant Ungilagtake and his lame-legged champion, though the younger brother dies of grief at his sister's grave on the way.
summary.zh: 兩名殷勤的孤兒在月光汲水時預見武裝大軍襲來；他們把幼妹藏入木屑堆、自己攀上椽木——七名來襲者屠戮全家，長矛更刺穿木屑下的幼妹。兄妹三人扶屍南逃，葬妹於巖洞，自此練成擲石碎熊之勇；投奔被「強者」害子的老人，娶其二女，以硬身術破強者的海象皮鞭，反以其道殺之，解放全村——『從此你們再無主子』——繼而南征巨人翁吉拉格塔克與其三舟而行的跛腿冠軍；然而弟弟因在妹妹墳前悲泣致病，未至目的地而亡。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as referring to Eskimo-Indian struggles and intertribal wars and migrations. Graphic violence recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Several men had their permanent winter-quarters near the entrance to a fiord, and with them lived two boys, very officious and obliging: in the morning they helped turn and rub the men's gloves, arranged the kayak implements and tools, fetched the water for their morning drink, exercised in archery all day, and carried their things from the beach at return. One evening in winter, by moonlight, drawing water, the youngest said, 'I think I see a lot of faces down in the water' — 'Is it not the reflection of the moon?' 'No, come and look for thyself' — and Kunuk, looking, saw by way of clairvoyance a host of armed men advancing towards them. They ran to tell the people at home, but were only told it must have been the moon that deceived them; seeing the armed men the third time, they deliberated what to do with their little sister, put her down in a heap of chips close to the window and covered her well up, then climbed the rafters beneath the roof of the house-passage, lying at full length, faces downwards, holding one beam with their hands and their feet against the next.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Presently a large man with a spear made his way through the entrance, then another; they counted seven, who came rushing into the house — and a fearful cry was heard from those who were put to death. While the raiders lingered inside, Kunuk's brother was losing strength; the aggressors came storming out, fighting right and left, flinging their spears everywhere, and likewise into the heap of chips where their little sister lay. When the last had disappeared the younger boy fell to the ground, Kunuk after him. They found their sister struck right through the body with a lance, entrails protruding; the house floor was all covered with blood, every one of the inmates killed, besides one of the assailants. Alone in the dreary house, they left the place that very night, carrying their wounded sister by turns and taking care the entrails did not come out of their proper place; they wandered on until, at a firth quite frozen over, past a steep promontory, their little sister died, and they buried her in a cave among the rocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.

passages.text: From the beginning of their flight they exercised themselves in boxing and lifting large stones to strengthen their limbs, and grew into strong and vigorous men ere they met other people again. A man on the ice beside a huge piece of hunting-wood adopted them as his sons, and their foster-parents encouraged them never to forget their enemies. They caught ptarmigan and foxes without any weapons by throwing large stones; practised boxing and wrestling, making a point never to fall but roll together along the ground; and at last grew so dexterous they could kill a bear without any weapon — giving him a blow, and when he turned upon them taking no more notice than if he had been a hare, merely taking hold of him by the legs and smashing him to pieces. They took a northerly direction and came at last to a great inlet where kayakers hunted seal — but only one of them, their chief or 'strong man,' was provided with weapons: the others had only to chase and frighten the animals, and anyone daring to wound them was punished by the chief in person. The brothers were too modest to go down at once, and meanwhile witnessed the cutting-up of a walrus, each person getting a huge piece excepting an old man in the poorest tent, who got nothing but the entrails, carried home from the beach by his two daughters. Taking pity on his patience, the brothers went to him in the dark; the old man offered them his daughters in marriage, Kunuk choosing the youngest, his brother the eldest — and thus they got married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Going down to the place they had examined the boats closely, and had taken the 'strong man's' javelin away with the intention of hiding it, sticking it so deep into hard dry turf by a spring that only what could be seized with two fingers was to be seen. An old gossip — mother to the 'strong man' — spied the strangers, and a multitude gathered at the tent entrance; in the morning the chief cried out that it was a fine day for a walrus-hunt, then fell silent: 'My javelin has been taken away.' All rushed to the rock leading to the spring to pull it out of the earth, but nobody succeeded, having pulled and bitten it until the end was quite wasted; Kunuk just took it between his two fingers and disengaged it as if it were a very small matter. Their father-in-law told them that under the great boat lay the perfectly fitted-up kayaks of his dead son, murdered by the 'strong man' who envied his still greater strength, making the old man the enemy of his own daughters. Then came the cry: 'Let the strangers come on for a boxing and fighting match on the great plain up yonder!' A pole was set up, beside it the leader with a whip of walrus-skin with a knot on the end, and a stuffed white hare — whoever set foot on it was quickly lashed. Kunuk was first; at the very moment the 'strong man' lifted his whip, Kunuk stooped and hardened his limbs by charm, so the whip gave a loud crack and Kunuk came away unhurt while the chief believed he had killed him. Then the chief proposed the younger brother take the whip for a change, went himself and put his foot on the hare — and Kunuk's brother, crying 'Look out and harden thy body!' smote him at the same time, so that he fell down dead on the spot. All his inferiors rejoiced greatly: 'Henceforth ye shall be our leaders!' — but the brothers rejoined, 'In future ye shall have no masters, but hunt at liberty and at your own will.' They practised all manner of kayaking feats with bladder-arrows of one entire blown-up seal-skin, and once lanced a very large she-walrus at greater distance than usual, the arrow going right through to the very vent-holes of the bladder. Hearing of the giant Ungilagtake, with his huge sword, from whom nobody was ever known to escape, they supposed him to have been among the armed men who attacked their housemates, and determined to find him out. But on the voyage south, Kunuk's brother, recognising the burial-place of their little sister on the land, sobbed bent over the helm, took ill from that very day, and died before they reached their destination, so that Kunuk came alone to Ungilagtake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the depth of winter they were met by many people on the ice, and a somewhat biggish man — himself an enemy of Ungilagtake — showed them how the giant used to behave to strangers: lifting an entire seal-skin stuffed with sand by a strap with his third finger, and challenging the guest to do the same (Kunuk lifted the thing with his little finger, unbent arm, and put it down without being fatigued), and throwing a lance at the stranger amid a song of 'Bend thee down, stranger!' — at which Kunuk bent so low nothing but his chin was visible, and the host lost his aim. Warned to make a bold entrance, Kunuk and his wife came up to a large house with three windows occupied by Ungilagtake's numerous stolen wives; refreshments were served, and when they had finished eating, Ungilagtake ordered Kunuk to seat himself opposite, drew out a huge spear from beneath the bench, struck the drum, and the whole joined in a song: 'Bend thee down, stranger that has come among us; the great Ungilagtake, who never missed his aim, is going to thrust his spear at thee.' He bent down, only his chin appearing — and whilst Ungilagtake took aim, Kunuk nimbly jumped and caught hold of one of the roof-beams, the spear going far below him; flung at a second time, he quickly jumped down and the spear came flying above him amid great cheers. Taking aim the third time, Kunuk seized the spear, saying he too would like to have a try at killing with it; they exchanged places, Kunuk struck up a song for Ungilagtake, and the very moment the giant prepared to bend his back, Kunuk had already taken aim — the spear hit him in the throat, and he fell dead on the spot. Everybody rushed out of the house, and Kunuk, following, found himself seized from behind by Tajangiarsuk, the giant's companion with a double back, immensely strong; on a plain of ice covered with projecting stones chosen on purpose to dash adversaries against, the wrestling-match began. Kunuk flung him down so the blood gushed out of his mouth; a still stronger and larger champion got Kunuk down, knee already on his heart, when Kunuk suddenly grasped his shoulders from beneath and pressed the lungs out of him; then came 'the last of the lot, him with the lame legs,' of such immense size that he had to lie across three boats to get along, creeping to the combat-field on his elbows. Kunuk whirled him round by the waist until his feet turned right outwards, letting him fall so that his skull was crushed. The people rejoiced and cried, 'Thanks to thee! now we shall have no masters!' — and those who had been robbed of their wives got them back again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.
